fetched_contents.text: Effectiveness of school-based interventions on fundamental movement skills in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Background Fundamental movement skills (FMS) are essential prerequisites for children’s active participation in physical activities (PA), which plays a crucial role in promoting both physical and mental health, ultimately contributing to their overall well-being. Children spend a significant portion of their time in school, making it a critical setting for the development of their FMS. However, systematic reviews and meta-analyses of the effects of school-based interventions on FMS have not been summarized. Therefore, the aim of this study was to analyze the effectiveness of school-based interventions on FMS in children. Methods This study employed a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies published between 2014 and 2024. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines were followed. A total of 15,930 publications were searched in the Web of Science (WOS), PubMed, and EBSCOhost databases. Two rounds of literature screening were conducted, including duplicate removal and title and abstract screening. Data analysis was conducted using Review Manager version 5.4, with meta-analysis performed using a random effects model. Publication bias was assessed using Stata version 18. The quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro) scale. Results A total of thirty-three studies from 14 countries were included in the analysis. Among them, thirty (90.91%) studies demonstrated that their interventions were effective. Thirty-one (93.94%) studies were implemented within classroom settings. Twenty-one (63.64%) studies had an intervention duration of less than 60 min. Twelve (36.36%) studies were conducted twice a week. Sixteen (48.48%) studies lasted less than 10 weeks. Meta-analysis of nine interventions indicated significant effects on overall FMS proficiency (SMD = 0.69, 95% CI = 0.21–1.16, I2 = 94%). Meta-analysis indicated that interventions with a duration of 60 min or more, a frequency of 3 times or more a week, and a period of 10 to 20 weeks were efficacious at enhancing FMS in children. Conclusions School-based interventions are effective in promoting children’s FMS. Long-duration, high-frequency, medium- and long-period interventions may be optimal for enhancing FMS. FMS can be categorized into three main types: locomotor skills (e.g., walking, running, jumping), object control skills (e.g., throwing, catching), and stability skills (e.g., balancing) [1]. These skills are considered primary predictors of children’s motor competence and are critical for the future acquisition of a diverse range of movement sequences. Proficiency in FMS plays a significant role in enhancing children’s PA, fosters self-perception, and supports executive function [2]. The development of FMS is closely linked to cardiorespiratory endurance and other health-related components [3–5]. A deficiency in FMS can impede the development of specific movement abilities in children, which can affect their participation in PA and can lead to various health-related issues, such as obesity. Current literature highlights the importance of FMS as a fundamental element in children’s overall growth and development. However, it’s concerning that the proficiency of FMS among children has declined in many countries [6, 7]. The acquisition of FMS is influenced by various factors in different environments. Factors such as the availability of exercise equipment and space within the school, family, and community play a significant role in the development of FMS [8]. It’s essential that teachers, parents, and other community members receive quality instruction, hands-on opportunities, feedback, and knowledge of FMS and education, as these factors can potentially influence the development of FMS [9]. Previous studies have summarized the effects of PA interventions, active play (AP) interventions, and some other interventions on FMS in different environments, demonstrating various interventions in different settings can promote the development of children’s FMS [10, 11]. No institution or environment has a greater influence on an individual during the first two decades of their life than the school [12]. On average, children spend a substantial portion of their time in school, approximately half of the year [13]. Furthermore, schools provide numerous opportunities for participation in various activities throughout the weekdays, including physical education (PE) classes and recess [14, 15]. Teacher training, education materials, and curriculum design are all crucial to promoting FMS, PA, and health-related content in school [12]. Moreover, the World Health Organization (WHO) has identified schools as critical environments for enhancing PA among children, advocating for curriculum-based interventions that address the entire student body to maximize intervention reach, while recommending that schools offer appropriate planning, opportunities, and diverse venues for PA [16]. Consequently, some countries, such as Poland [17] and the United States [18], are evaluating the relationship between the proficiency of FMS and PE classes, Furthermore, in China, FMS is listed as part of the compulsory education standards [19].
